Fairbairn-Sykes Fighting Knife

The Fairbairn-Sykes Fighting Knife is a double-edged combat dagger featuring a foil-style grip, designed by William Ewart Fairbairn and Eric Anthony Sykes. The F-S knife was engineered exclusively for surprise attacks and close-quarters combat. A key advantage of its slender blade is its ability to easily slip between ribs. The ceramic handle ensures a firm grip, while the needle-pointed blade profile makes it an outstanding combat dagger. Highly lethal in close combat, a well-placed strike to the heart can cause a target to bleed out within 2 to 5 seconds.

Desert Eagle Mark XIX

The Desert Eagle is a large-caliber semi-automatic pistol, positioned primarily as a civilian hunting sidearm. Designed in 1983 in the United States by Magnum Research and later refined by Israel Military Industries, the Mark XIX is based on the earlier Mark VII model. It is produced in variants chambered for .357 Magnum, .44 Magnum, and .50 Action Express, with 6- or 10-inch barrels. Mention was also made of a version chambered in .440 Cor-bon. Desert Eagle pistols are extremely sensitive to maintenance and have never been tested for harsh environmental performance, as they were engineered as specialized hunting handguns rather than military service sidearms.

1887 Nagant

The Nagant M1887 revolver, an innovative development by Belgian brothers Emile and Leon Nagant, is a unique and powerful sidearm featuring an unprecedented gas-seal system. This seven-shot double-action revolver is famous for its ability to maintain a completely gas-tight seal between the cylinder and barrel, increasing muzzle velocity and overall accuracy. Adopted by the Russian Empire, the revolver features a rugged frame, a distinctive loading gate on the right side, and an integrated folding ejector rod. Its robust design and reliable action made it a favorite among military and law enforcement personnel, highly valued for its precision and durability.

AMP Auto Mag pistol

The .44 Auto Mag pistol (AMP) is a large-caliber semi-automatic sidearm. Developed between 1966 and 1971 by the Auto Mag Corporation, it was engineered to create a semi-automatic handgun chambered in .44 AMP. The pistol's reputation and distinctive appearance made it popular in cinema and fiction, with several variants listed as "Curios and Relics" by the ATF. The short-recoil operated Auto Mag utilizes a rotating bolt with six locking lugs located at the front, similar to the M16/AR-15 platform. The Auto Mag is a lightweight pistol designed to grant .44 Magnum revolver firepower in a semi-automatic platform. The .44 Auto Mag round was engineered to push a .429-inch 240-grain bullet at roughly the same velocity as a .44 Magnum revolver. A bold Zone technician rechambered this model to .357 to utilize the far more common ammunition found across the Zone.\n \n
Beretta 92FS

The 92FS is the refined evolution of the Italian 9x19mm semi-automatic Beretta 92 pistol, manufactured by Fabbrica d'Armi Pietro Beretta in 1975. One of its most distinctive design traits is the open-slide design with no feed ramp, featuring substantial iron sights for its era and utilizing double-stack magazines holding 15 rounds each. In service across numerous countries for military, law enforcement, and civilian applications alike, it remains one of the most reliable high-capacity 9x19mm handguns you will ever handle in the Zone.

7.62mm PKP «Pecheneg» machine gun is a Russian general-purpose machine gun developed based on the PKM. Designed to engage enemy personnel, firing points, vehicles, and aerial targets. An adjustable gas regulator allows operating the «Pecheneg» in any climatic conditions. The barrel has external ribbing and is enclosed in a metal shroud. Powder gases leaving the muzzle create a vacuum zone at the front of the shroud. Special ventilation ports are made in the rear of the shroud.  The StG 44 was the first successful assault rifle, featuring key characteristics such as an intermediate cartridge (7.92x33mm Kurz), controllable automatic fire, a more compact build than traditional battle rifles, higher rate of fire, and primary optimization for engaging targets within a few hundred meters. Other service rifles of the era were designed to engage targets beyond a thousand meters, which was found to exceed the range at which actual infantry combat occurred.
 
 The StG 44 served its role effectively, particularly on the Eastern Front, providing significantly greater firepower compared to standard infantry rifles. The StG heavily influenced the Soviet AK-47 assault rifle introduced two years after the war. Its legacy remains evident in modern assault rifles, which became the global standard for infantry small arms following WWII.

RPG-29 «Vampir»

The RPG-29 "Vampir" is a man-portable anti-tank grenade launcher (RPG)[cite: 8]. Developed between 1983 and 1989 by GNPP "Bazalt" (GSKB-47, Chief Designer A.N. Obukhov, Designer V.S. Tokarev) and TsKIB SOO (Designers V.I. Matveev, V.I. Zaitsev) under the designation TKB-0175, based on the RPG-16[cite: 8]. Designed for a new generation of tandem-charge HEAT grenades[cite: 8]. Fiberglass solid-propellant rocket motors for its ammunition entered mass production in 1986 (developed by NPO "Altay", Biysk)[cite: 8]. Adopted into service in 1989 firing the PG-29V tandem-charge rocket[cite: 8]. Manufactured by the "Molot" Machine-Building Plant, a trial batch was produced for export, though full serial production for USSR/Russian forces was never initiated[cite: 8]. First revealed to international media at the IDEX-93 defense exhibition in Abu Dhabi in 1993[cite: 8].

Its compact footprint and light weight make it an essential asset for deep raids into the Zone[cite: 8].
